claim: Tenectin (Tnc) is a Mucin-type protein with RGD motifs.
source: Here we report that Tenectin (Tnc), a Mucin-type protein with RGD motifs, is an ECM component required for the structural and functional integrity of synaptic specializations at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in Drosophila.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the protein domain diagram in Figure 1B showing PTS domains and RGD motifs.

claim: Tnc is an ECM component required for the structural and functional integrity of synaptic specializations at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: Here we report that Tenectin (Tnc), a Mucin-type protein with RGD motifs, is an ECM component required for the structural and functional integrity of synaptic specializations at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including genetics, biochemistry, electrophysiology, histology and electron microscopy described throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tnc is secreted from motor neurons and striated muscles.
source: Using genetics, biochemistry, electrophysiology, histology and electron microscopy, we show that Tnc is secreted from motor neurons and striated muscles and accumulates in the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis showing Tnc in both brain and muscle extracts (Figure 1C), and by S2 cell secretion assays (Figure 1D).

claim: Tnc accumulates in the synaptic cleft.
source: Using genetics, biochemistry, electrophysiology, histology and electron microscopy, we show that Tnc is secreted from motor neurons and striated muscles and accumulates in the synaptic cleft.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry showing Tnc signals at NMJ boutons (Figure 1F-J) and detergent-free staining showing extracellular localization (Figure 1I).

claim: Tnc selectively recruits αPS2/βPS integrin at synaptic terminals.
source: Tnc selectively recruits αPS2/βPS integrin at synaptic terminals, but only the cis Tnc/integrin complexes appear to be biologically active.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dramatic reduction of βPS and αPS2 (but not αPS1) at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 4A-D, I-K), and by proximity ligation assays showing Tnc and βPS in close proximity (Figure 4G-H).

claim: Only cis Tnc/integrin complexes are biologically active.
source: Tnc selectively recruits αPS2/βPS integrin at synaptic terminals, but only the cis Tnc/integrin complexes appear to be biologically active.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments showing that neuronal Tnc can recruit postsynaptic βPS but cannot restore bouton size, whereas muscle Tnc can rescue both (Figure 7).

claim: Presynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes control neurotransmitter release.
source: These complexes have distinct pre- and postsynaptic functions, mediated at least in part through the local engagement of the spectrin-based membrane skeleton: the presynaptic complexes control neurotransmitter release, while postsynaptic complexes ensure the size and architectural integrity of synaptic boutons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology showing reduced mEJP frequency and EJP amplitude in tnc mutants (Figure 2), and by neuronal knockdown of tnc or mys/βPS producing similar defects (Figure 3).

claim: Postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes ensure the size and architectural integrity of synaptic boutons.
source: These complexes have distinct pre- and postsynaptic functions, mediated at least in part through the local engagement of the spectrin-based membrane skeleton: the presynaptic complexes control neurotransmitter release, while postsynaptic complexes ensure the size and architectural integrity of synaptic boutons.
evidence: This is supported by smaller boutons and reduced Dlg signals in tnc mutants (Figure 5A-G), sparse SSR in electron micrographs (Figure 5H-J), and muscle-specific knockdown recapitulating these defects (Figure 5C-E).

claim: Integrin has a role in the synaptic recruitment of spectrin-based membrane skeleton.
source: Our study reveals an unprecedented role for integrin in the synaptic recruitment of spectrin-based membrane skeleton.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dramatic reduction of α-Spectrin and Adducin at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 6D-I), and by muscle knockdown of mys/βPS reducing α-Spectrin accumulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H).

claim: tnc was identified in a synthetic lethality screen with neto109.
source: We uncovered tnc, which encodes a developmentally regulated RGD-containing integrin ligand (Fraichard et al., 2006; Fraichard et al., 2010), in a screen for ECM candidates that interact genetically with neto, a gene essential for NMJ assembly and function (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: The screen methodology is described in the Results section, where deficiencies disrupting tnc increased lethality of neto109 hemizygotes from 50% to 82%.

claim: Tnc encodes a developmentally regulated RGD-containing integrin ligand.
source: We uncovered tnc, which encodes a developmentally regulated RGD-containing integrin ligand (Fraichard et al., 2006; Fraichard et al., 2010), in a screen for ECM candidates that interact genetically with neto, a gene essential for NMJ assembly and function (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and by the protein structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Tnc is a large mucin-type protein conserved in many insects but with no obvious mammalian homologue.
source: Among the common loci disrupted by these deficiencies was tnc, a gene coding for a large mucin-type protein conserved in many insects but with no obvious mammalian homologue (Figure 1A–B) (Fraichard et al., 2006; Syed et al., 2008; Fraichard et al., 2010; Syed et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated directly and supported by citations to previous characterization studies.

claim: Tnc has five vWFC domains, Pro/Thr/Ser-rich mucin specific domains, and RGD motifs.
source: Tnc is a secreted molecule with five vWFC (von Willebrand factor type-C) protein interaction domains separated by two PTS-rich regions. In mucins, the PTS domains are highly O-glycosylated and form gel-like structures. Tnc has one RGD and several more RGD-like motifs that have been implicated in interaction with integrin (Fraichard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is described in the text and illustrated in the protein domain diagram in Figure 1B.

claim: During development, Tnc is secreted in the lumen of several epithelial organs, including foregut, hindgut and trachea.
source: During development, Tnc is secreted in the lumen of several epithelial organs, including foregut, hindgut and trachea.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text.

claim: Tnc is expressed in the embryonic CNS.
source: Tnc is also expressed in the embryonic CNS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining showing Tnc signals enriched in the neuropile near FasII-positive axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: Tnc signals are strongly enriched in the neuropile, in the proximity of anti-Fasciclin II positive axons.
source: Using a polyclonal anti-Tnc antibody (Materials and methods) we found that Tnc signals are strongly enriched in the neuropile, in the proximity of the anti-Fasciclin II (FasII) positive axons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B and [Fraichard et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B with immunostaining of embryos.

claim: Tnc signals are absent in the CNS of tnc mutant embryos.
source: The Tnc signals were absent in the CNS of a tnc mutant (tncEP- P[EPgy2]EY03355), predicted to disrupt both known tnc transcripts (Syed et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B demonstrating antibody specificity.

claim: tnc mutant embryos have a normal FasII pattern indicating no obvious CNS defects during late embryogenesis.
source: These mutant embryos had a normal FasII pattern indicating no obvious CNS defects during late embryogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining of FasII-positive longitudinal axon tracks in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The tncEP mutant shows partial lethality with 11.6% of expected homozygous progenies viable.
source: The tncEP mutant showed partial lethality (11.6% of expected homozygous progenies were viable, n = 303), which was not enhanced in heteroallelic combinations (12.2% viability for tncEP/Df, n = 392) suggesting that this mutant is equivalent to a genetic null.
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and counting of progeny.

claim: tncEP is equivalent to a genetic null allele.
source: The tncEP mutant showed partial lethality (11.6% of expected homozygous progenies were viable, n = 303), which was not enhanced in heteroallelic combinations (12.2% viability for tncEP/Df, n = 392) suggesting that this mutant is equivalent to a genetic null.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of enhancement in heteroallelic combinations.

claim: tnc82 mutant animals die as homozygous pharate adults with 100% lethality.
source: We also generated a small deletion mutant (tnc82) by FRT-induced recombination. These animals die as homozygous pharate adults (100% lethality, n = 221) but produce some heteroallelic escapers (17.5% viability for tnc82/Df, n = 389).
evidence: This is based on genetic crosses and counting of progeny.

claim: Western blot analysis reveals a Tnc-positive band of ~300 kD in extracts from brains and body-wall muscles of control larvae.
source: Western blot analysis revealed a Tnc-positive band of ~300 kD (the calculated MW for Tnc is 299 kD) in extracts from brains and body-wall muscles of control larvae (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot in Figure 1C.

claim: The Tnc band is undetectable in tnc hetero-allelic combinations tncEP/Df and tnc82/Df.
source: This band was undetectable in tnc hetero-allelic combinations, tncEP/Df and tnc82/Df.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot in Figure 1C demonstrating loss of protein in mutants.

claim: Tnc is efficiently secreted in S2 cell culture media.
source: A band of similar size was found in S2 cells transfected with a Tnc expression construct and was enriched in the conditioned media, indicating that Tnc is efficiently secreted in cell culture (Figure 1D, Material and methods).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot showing Tnc enriched in media (S) compared to cell pellet (P) in Figure 1D.

claim: Neuron specific RNAi knockdown reduces Tnc levels in larval brains to 43% of the control group.
source: Neuron specific RNAi knockdown reduced Tnc levels in larval brains to 43% of the control group; this generated very strong phenotypes (below) suggesting that the residual band could reflect additional Tnc-expressing cells in the larval brain.
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot in Figure 1E.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown reduces muscle Tnc levels to 19% of the control.
source: The muscle-specific knockdown reduced the muscle Tnc levels to 19% of the control (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot in Figure 1E.

claim: During larval stages, Tnc positive signals are found throughout the muscles with weak accumulation at the NMJ.
source: During larval stages, we found Tnc positive signals throughout the muscles with weak accumulation at the NMJ (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Tnc signals are significantly reduced at tncEP/Df mutant NMJs compared to controls.
source: Under the same imaging conditions, the signals were significantly reduced in tncEP/Df mutants (Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E,G.

claim: Paneuronal expression of Tnc induces strong accumulation of Tnc-positive signals at synaptic terminals and along motor neuron axons.
source: Paneuronal expression of Tnc induced strong accumulation of Tnc-positive signals at synaptic terminals, as well as along the motor neuron axons.
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: At NMJs with neuronal Tnc overexpression, Tnc-labeled puncta are concentrated at the edge of anti-HRP-stained boutons.
source: At these NMJs, Tnc-labeled puncta were concentrated at the edge of anti-horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-stained boutons (Jan and Jan, 1982).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H with immunostaining.

claim: Most Tnc signals from neuronal overexpression are observed in the absence of detergents, suggesting that Tnc is secreted in the synaptic terminal.
source: Most of these signals were also observed in the absence of detergents, suggesting that Tnc is secreted in the synaptic terminal.
evidence: This is demonstrated by detergent-free staining in Figure 1I showing extracellular Tnc puncta.

claim: Muscle overexpression of tnc shows increased Tnc-positive signals throughout the muscle with diffuse signals at synaptic terminals.
source: In contrast, muscle overexpression of tnc showed increased Tnc-positive signals throughout the muscle; at synaptic terminals these signals appeared diffuse and farther away from the neuronal membrane.
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 1J and Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Excess muscle Tnc may not be properly targeted and/or stabilized at synaptic terminals.
source: Thus, excess muscle Tnc may not be properly targeted and/or stabilized at synaptic terminals and may have detrimental effects on Tnc-mediated functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the diffuse distribution of Tnc when overexpressed in muscle compared to the punctate accumulation with neuronal overexpression.

claim: Both HA-tagged and untagged tnc transgenes rescue the viability of tnc mutants.
source: Both tagged and untagged transgenes rescued the viability of tnc mutants (see below), indicating that Tnc functions are unaffected by addition of the tag.
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated by rescue experiments described later.

claim: Expression of tnc-HA in neurons but not in muscles induces high accumulation of HA-positive puncta around synaptic boutons.
source: As above, expression of tnc-HA in neurons but not in muscles induced high accumulation of HA-positive puncta, accessible without detergent, around the synaptic boutons, indicating extracellular distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: tnc mutants have largely normal NMJ morphology during larval stages with minimally increased bouton numbers.
source: During larval stages, both tnc mutants (tncEP/Df and tnc82/Df) had largely normal NMJ, with minimally increased bouton numbers (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is shown by HRP staining and quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: tnc mutants have smaller boutons with less clear bouton-interbouton delimitations.
source: A closer examination revealed smaller boutons, with less clear bouton-interbouton delimitations (details below).
evidence: This is described in the text and detailed in later sections with Dlg staining (Figure 5).

claim: Adult tnc escapers do not fly and exhibit climbing defects.
source: The few adult escapers did not fly and exhibited climbing defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by climbing assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mEJPs amplitude is normal in tnc mutants.
source: The mEJPs amplitude was normal in tnc mutants.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 2C.

claim: The mean frequency of mEJPs is significantly reduced in tnc mutants compared to control.
source: However, the mean frequency of mEJPs was significantly reduced in tnc mutants compared with the control (w1118, 2.67 ± 0.14 Hz vs. tncEP/Df, 1.68 ± 0.13 Hz, p=0.0001, and tnc82/Df, 2.11 ± 0.14 Hz, p=0.0322, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings and quantification in Figure 2A,D.

claim: tnc mutations cause 23% and 18% reduction in evoked EJPs amplitude of tncEP/Df and tnc82/Df animals, respectively.
source: tnc mutations caused 23% and 18% reduction in evoked EJPs amplitude of tncEP/Df and tnc82/Df animals, respectively (w1118, 26.30 ± 0.99 mV vs. tncEP/Df, 20.15 ± 1.26 mV, p=0.0042, and tnc82/Df, 21.53 ± 1.38 mV, p=0.0375, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings and quantification in Figure 2B,E.

claim: tnc mutants show a significant decrease in quantal content.
source: Moreover, tnc mutants showed a significant decrease in quantal content (w1118, 29.05 ± 1.81 vs. tncEP/Df, 21.44 ± 1.60 and tnc82/Df, 21.53 ± 1.38, Figure 2F).
evidence: This is calculated from EJP and mEJP data and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is no change in resting potential and input resistance in tnc mutant animals.
source: Since we found no change in the resting potential and input resistance in mutant animals, the decrease in EJPs amplitude and quantal content was probably not caused by abnormal passive membrane properties in the muscle.
evidence: Resting potential and input resistance values are provided in the Figure 2 legend showing no significant differences.

claim: The reduction of quantal content in tnc mutants could be due to a decreased number of vesicle release sites or reduced probability of release.
source: Instead, the reduction of quantal content could be due to a decreased number of vesicle release sites or reduced probability of release.
evidence: This is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing reduced quantal content.

claim: Control larvae show mild short-term depression following paired-pulse stimulation at 0.5 mM extracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: At 0.5 mM extracellular Ca2+ concentration, the control larvae showed mild short-term depression following paired-pulse stimulation (PPR < 1, Figure 2G–H), indicating a relatively high initial probability of vesicle release
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired-pulse recordings in Figure 2G-H.

claim: tnc mutant NMJs show elevated facilitation and significantly increased paired-pulse ratio.
source: In contrast, the tnc mutant NMJs showed elevated facilitation and significantly increased PPR (w1118, 0.80 ± 0.03 vs. tncEP/Df, 1.21 ± 0.08, p=0.0231, and tnc82/Df, 1.16 ± 0.09, p=0.0295).
evidence: This is demonstrated by paired-pulse recordings and quantification in Figure 2G-H.

claim: tnc mutants have significantly decreased probability of vesicle release.
source: The higher the ratio of EJP amplitudes following the first and second pulses, the lower is the probability of release. Thus, tnc mutants have significantly decreased probability of vesicle release.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased paired-pulse ratio in tnc mutants.

claim: Neuronal knockdown of tnc significantly reduces mEJPs frequency compared to controls.
source: We found that tnc knockdown in motor neurons resulted in mEJPs with significantly reduced frequency as compared to the controls (tncRNAi transgene with no driver, or driver alone) (control, 2.69 ± 0.2 Hz vs. N > tncRNAi, 1.31 ± 0.10 Hz p=0.0001, and M > tncRNAi, 2.4 ± 0.17 Hz p=0.4434) (Figure 3A–C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Muscle knockdown of tnc has no effect on mEJPs frequency or amplitude.
source: In contrast, tnc knockdown in muscles had no effect on mEJPs frequency or amplitude.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Neuronal but not muscle Tnc is required for normal neurotransmitter release.
source: Thus, neuronal but not muscle Tnc is required for normal neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is concluded from the tissue-specific knockdown experiments showing only neuronal knockdown affects mEJP frequency.

claim: Expression of Tnc in neurons but not in muscles rescues the mEJPs frequency and EJPs amplitude defects in tnc mutants.
source: Expression of Tnc in neurons but not in muscles also rescued the mEJPs frequency and EJPs amplitude defects observed in tnc mutants (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments and electrophysiology in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Neuronal knockdown of mys/βPS integrin significantly reduces mEJPs frequency compared to control.
source: Indeed, neuronal knockdown of myospheroid (mys), which encodes the βPS integrin subunit, significantly reduced the mEJPs frequency compared to control (mysRNAi transgene with no driver) (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Muscle knockdown of mys has no detectable effect on mEJPs frequency or amplitude.
source: In contrast, muscle knockdown of mys had no detectable effect on mEJPs frequency (control, 0.95 ± 0.14 Hz vs. N > mysRNAi, 0.47 ± 0.05 Hz p=0.0044 and M > mysRNAi, 1.00 ± 0.07 Hz p=0.9142) or amplitude.
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Neuronal but not muscle knockdown of if/αPS2 integrin significantly reduces mEJPs frequency compared to control.
source: Similarly, neuronal but not muscle knockdown of inflated (if), which codes for αPS2 integrin, significantly reduced the mEJPs frequency compared to control (ifRNAi transgene with no driver) (Figure 3J–L) (control, 1.62 ± 0.51 Hz vs. N > ifRNAi, 0.99 ± 0.23 Hz p=0.0041 and M > ifRNAi, 1.67 ± 0.42 Hz p=0.9662).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3J-L.

claim: Knockdown of if/αPS2 induces slight reduction of mEJPs amplitude and occasionally muscle attachment defects.
source: The ifRNAi transgene appeared stronger than mysRNAi and generated larval lethality and, occasionally, muscle attachment defects; using these transgenes we observed diminished mEJP amplitude compared to control (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is shown in the electrophysiology data in Figure 3L.

claim: Neuron-derived Tnc functions as a ligand for presynaptic αPS2/βPS to modulate neurotransmitter release.
source: Overall, the reduction of presynaptic αPS2/βPS mirrored the mEJP frequency deficits observed for tnc neuronal knockdown suggesting that neuron-derived Tnc functions as a ligand for presynaptic αPS2/βPS to modulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is inferred from the parallel phenotypes of tnc and integrin knockdowns in neurons.

claim: Postsynaptic αPS2/βPS integrin does not appear to influence neurotransmitter release.
source: Postsynaptic αPS2/βPS integrin does not appear to influence neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is concluded from the lack of effect of muscle knockdown of mys or if on mEJP frequency.

claim: Trans-heterozygotes (mys/+;; tnc/+) exhibit severe mEJP deficits that resemble tnc mutants.
source: Indeed, these trans-heterozygotes exhibited severe mEJP deficits that resembled tnc mutants, whereas individual heterozygote larvae (mys/+ or tnc/+) showed normal mEJPs frequency and amplitude (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings in Figure 3M-O showing genetic interaction.

claim: tnc and mys function together to modulate neurotransmitter release.
source: This indicates that tnc and mys function together to modulate neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic interaction between tnc and mys heterozygotes.

claim: βPS signals are dramatically reduced at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: Indeed, the βPS signals were dramatically reduced at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4A-D,P.

claim: βPS immunoreactivities concentrate at perisynaptic locations, surrounding control boutons.
source: In these analyses the βPS immunoreactivities concentrated at perisynaptic locations, surrounding the control boutons, consistent with previous observations that the muscle pool constitutes the major fraction of βPS at synaptic terminals (Beumer et al., 1999).
evidence: This is shown in the immunostaining images in Figure 4A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: βPS levels remain unchanged at muscle attachment sites in tnc mutants.
source: Interestingly, the βPS levels remained unchanged at the muscle attachment sites; we also observed no detachment of the muscle fibers or defects in costamere organization (Maartens and Brown, 2015).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B,D with arrows indicating normal βPS at muscle attachment sites.

claim: Loss of Tnc selectively impairs the recruitment of βPS integrin at synaptic terminals.
source: This indicates that loss of Tnc selectively impairs the recruitment of βPS integrin at synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is concluded from the selective loss of βPS at NMJs but not at muscle attachment sites in tnc mutants.

claim: Anti-Tnc antibodies mark discrete puncta at the edge of HRP-labeled boutons in a region strongly stained by anti-βPS antibodies.
source: The anti-Tnc antibodies marked discrete puncta at the edge of the HRP- labeled boutons in a region strongly stained by anti-βPS antibodies, but Tnc was not detectable at the muscle attachment sites (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is shown by co-immunostaining in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Tnc and βPS may directly associate at synaptic terminals.
source: This suggests that Tnc and βPS may directly associate at synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of Tnc and βPS at the edge of boutons.

claim: PLA signals between Tnc and βPS are detected at control but not at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: As shown in Figure 4G–H, PLA signals between Tnc and βPS were detected at control but not at tnc mutant NMJs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by proximity ligation assay in Figure 4G-H'.

claim: PLA signals between Tnc and βPS are tightly packed around synaptic boutons.
source: These PLA signals were tightly packed around the synaptic boutons, unlike the Tnc or βPS immunoreactivities, which spread into the postsynaptic specializations, suggesting that Tnc and βPS form complexes in the close proximity of the synaptic terminal.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4G' with PLA signals concentrated circumferentially around boutons.

claim: Tnc and βPS form complexes in close proximity of the synaptic terminal.
source: These PLA signals were tightly packed around the synaptic boutons, unlike the Tnc or βPS immunoreactivities, which spread into the postsynaptic specializations, suggesting that Tnc and βPS form complexes in the close proximity of the synaptic terminal.
evidence: This is inferred from the PLA results showing Tnc and βPS within 40 nm of each other.

claim: αPS2 but not αPS1 levels are selectively reduced at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: We found that αPS2 but not αPS1 levels were selectively reduced at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 4I–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B), consistent with the RGD-containing Tnc being a ligand for αPS2/βPS (Fraichard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4I-K,P and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B,G.

claim: The levels of phosphorylated Fak are normal at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: In addition, the levels of phosphorylated Fak were normal at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D) suggesting that Tnc does not influence the LanA-induced αPS3/βν activation of the Fak signaling pathway (Tsai et al., 2008; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D,G.

claim: FasII synaptic levels are increased by 40% in tnc mutants compared with controls.
source: We found that FasII synaptic levels were increased by 40% (p<0.05, n = 28) in tnc mutants compared with the controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F,G.

claim: The increase in FasII at tnc mutant NMJs resembles the elevated levels of FasII reported at mys mutant NMJs.
source: This increase resembles the elevated levels of FasII reported at mys mutant NMJs, and indicates that loss of Tnc recapitulates some of the phenotypes reported for selective mys mutants (Beumer et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated with reference to published literature on mys mutants.

claim: tnc knockdown in muscles, but not in neurons, reduces synaptic βPS levels.
source: However, we found that tnc knockdown in muscles, but not in neurons, reduced the synaptic βPS levels (Figure 4M–O, quantified in P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue-specific knockdown and immunostaining in Figure 4M-O,P.

claim: tnc knockdown in neurons induces a significant increase of βPS synaptic levels.
source: In fact, tnc knockdown in neurons induced a significant increase of βPS synaptic levels, suggesting that neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of predominantly postsynaptic βPS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4N,P with quantification.

claim: Neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of predominantly postsynaptic βPS.
source: In fact, tnc knockdown in neurons induced a significant increase of βPS synaptic levels, suggesting that neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of predominantly postsynaptic βPS.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in βPS when neuronal Tnc is knocked down.

claim: tnc knockdown in motor neurons produces a significant increase (by 28%) of synaptic Tnc levels.
source: Compared to the control (tncRNAi transgene with no driver), tnc knockdown in motor neurons produced a significant increase (by 28%, p=0.0044, n = 27) of synaptic Tnc levels
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,E.

claim: Neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of muscle-derived Tnc at synaptic terminals.
source: Thus, neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of muscle-derived Tnc at synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is concluded from the increase in synaptic Tnc when neuronal Tnc is knocked down.

claim: tnc knockdown in muscle diminishes synaptic Tnc levels by 37%.
source: In contrast, tnc knockdown in muscle diminished the synaptic Tnc levels by 37% (p<0.0001, n = 30).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,E.

claim: Muscle Tnc is required in cis for the postsynaptic recruitment of βPS.
source: Nonetheless our data indicate that muscle Tnc is required in cis for the postsynaptic recruitment of βPS and that neuron-derived Tnc limits the accumulation of both Tnc and βPS postsynaptically (see below).
evidence: This is concluded from the tissue-specific knockdown experiments showing muscle Tnc is necessary for βPS accumulation.

claim: Lack of Tnc does not alter the intensities of GluRIIA and GluRIIB synaptic signals or the IIA/IIB ratio.
source: Lack of Tnc did not alter the intensities of GluRIIA and GluRIIB synaptic signals or the IIA/IIB ratio (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B,E.

claim: This result is consistent with the normal mini amplitude observed at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: This result is consistent with the normal mini amplitude observed at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 2).
evidence: This connects the normal glutamate receptor levels with the normal mEJP amplitude.

claim: Neto appears properly recruited at Tnc-depleted synapses.
source: Neto itself appeared properly recruited at Tnc-depleted synapses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D,E.

claim: PAK signals are normal at Tnc-deprived NMJs.
source: We found that PAK signals are normal at Tnc-deprived NMJs, even though the βPS levels are reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-D,E.

claim: tnc mutant NMJs have smaller boutons and diminished Dlg signals.
source: In the absence of Tnc, the type Ib boutons appeared significantly smaller and had diminished Dlg signals (Figure 5A–B, quantified in F-G).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 5A-B,F-G.

claim: tnc knockdown in neurons induces a slight increase in Dlg signals and no change in bouton area.
source: tnc knockdown in neurons induced a slight increase in the Dlg signals and no change in the bouton area, whereas tnc knockdown in muscles significantly decreased both the Dlg synaptic levels and the size of the type Ib boutons (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is shown by tissue-specific knockdown and immunostaining in Figure 5C-E,F-G.

claim: tnc knockdown in muscles significantly decreases both Dlg synaptic levels and the size of type Ib boutons.
source: tnc knockdown in neurons induced a slight increase in the Dlg signals and no change in the bouton area, whereas tnc knockdown in muscles significantly decreased both the Dlg synaptic levels and the size of the type Ib boutons (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is shown by tissue-specific knockdown and immunostaining in Figure 5C-E,F-G.

claim: Postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes control bouton size.
source: Similar reduction in bouton size has been reported for selective mys mutants (Beumer et al., 1999), suggesting that postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes control bouton size.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity to published mys mutant phenotypes and the muscle-specific requirement for Tnc.

claim: tnc mutants have sparse SSR with reduced density of membrane layers.
source: The tnc mutants have sparse SSR with reduced density of the membrane layers (quantified in I).
evidence: This is shown by electron microscopy in Figure 5H-J with quantification in 5I.

claim: The tnc synapses appear normal but reside in relatively distorted boutons.
source: The tnc synapses appear normal (insert detail) but they reside in relatively distorted boutons.
evidence: This is shown in the electron micrographs in Figure 5J with normal synaptic structures but irregular bouton shapes.

claim: The mutant boutons have irregular shapes and are surrounded by sparse SSR, with wider spaces between the membrane layers.
source: However, the mutant boutons had irregular shapes and were surrounded by sparse SSR, with wider spaces between the membrane layers.
evidence: This is shown in the electron micrographs in Figure 5J.

claim: Muscle Tnc regulates the SSR thickness and bouton architecture.
source: These ultrastructural defects are consistent with the observed morphological phenotypes and indicate that muscle Tnc regulates the SSR thickness and bouton architecture.
evidence: This is concluded from the EM data showing SSR defects and the tissue-specific knockdown showing muscle Tnc is required.

claim: Mature microtubule bundles at tnc mutant NMJs remain organized in smooth sheaths and loops, similar to control.
source: These microtubules remained organized in smooth sheaths and loops in tnc mutant larvae, similar to the control.
evidence: This is shown by Futsch staining in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Loss of tnc severely disrupts α-Spectrin accumulation at the NMJs.
source: In contrast, loss of tnc severely disrupted the α-Spectrin accumulation at the NMJs (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Net levels of α-Spectrin are normal in extracts from tnc larval muscles.
source: The net levels of α-Spectrin were normal in extracts from tnc larval muscles, as determined by Western blot analysis, but the synaptic abundance of α-Spectrin at tnc NMJs was reduced to 37% from control levels (p<0.001, n = 21).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot in Figure 6C and immunostaining quantification in Figure 6F.

claim: The synaptic abundance of α-Spectrin at tnc NMJs is reduced to 37% from control levels.
source: The net levels of α-Spectrin were normal in extracts from tnc larval muscles, as determined by Western blot analysis, but the synaptic abundance of α-Spectrin at tnc NMJs was reduced to 37% from control levels (p<0.001, n = 21).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Loss of synaptic α-Spectrin is consistent with the sparse SSR observed at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: Since α-Spectrin is essential for the integrity of the SSR (Pielage et al., 2006), loss of synaptic α-Spectrin is consistent with the sparse SSR observed at tnc mutant NMJs.
evidence: This connects the α-Spectrin reduction with the SSR defects through cited literature.

claim: α- and β-spectrin mutant embryos have reduced neurotransmitter release and diminished EJPs amplitudes without apparent defects in postsynaptic receptor fields.
source: Moreover, α- and β-spectrin mutant embryos have reduced neurotransmitter release and diminished EJPs amplitudes without any apparent defects in postsynaptic receptor fields (Featherstone et al., 2001); these defects are reminiscent of Tnc-deprived NMJs.
evidence: This comparison is made to cited literature on spectrin mutants.

claim: The distorted shapes of tnc mutant boutons resemble the less individuated boutons seen in α-spectrinR22S larvae.
source: Interestingly, the distorted shapes of tnc mutant boutons resemble the less individuated boutons seen in α-spectrinR22S larvae, which are impaired for spectrin tetramerization (Khanna et al., 2015).
evidence: This comparison is made to cited literature on spectrin tetramerization mutants.

claim: Adducin is diminished at tnc mutant terminals.
source: Using this antibody, we found that Adducin is also diminished at tnc mutant terminals (Figure 6G–I).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Tnc is required for the proper recruitment of SBMS at the NMJ.
source: These data suggest that Tnc is required for the proper recruitment of SBMS at the NMJ.
evidence: This is concluded from the reduction of α-Spectrin and Adducin at tnc mutant NMJs.

claim: The accumulation of α-Spectrin at synaptic terminals is limited by neuronal Tnc and promoted by muscle-derived Tnc.
source: Similar to βPS, the accumulation of α-Spectrin at synaptic terminals appeared to be limited by neuronal Tnc and promoted by muscle-derived Tnc, as indicated by knockdown analyses (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is shown by tissue-specific knockdown experiments in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Changes in synaptic α-Spectrin levels follow the variations in integrin levels at synaptic terminals.
source: Moreover, the changes in synaptic α-Spectrin levels followed the variations in integrin levels at synaptic terminals, since manipulations of mys/(βPS) elicited a similar profile for the synaptic α-Spectrin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: This is shown by mys knockdown experiments in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: Postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes function to recruit the SBMS at synaptic terminals.
source: Together our data suggest that the postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes function to recruit the SBMS at synaptic terminals; this activity seems restricted by neuron-derived Tnc, which appears to limit the accumulation and function of postsynaptic complexes.
evidence: This is concluded from the tissue-specific effects on integrin and spectrin accumulation.

claim: Complete loss of Tnc triggers severe reduction of integrin and α-Spectrin at synaptic terminals.
source: Complete loss of Tnc triggers severe reduction of integrin and α-Spectrin at synaptic terminals, consistent with the observed disruption of bouton architecture.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from tnc mutant analysis.

claim: Paneuronal expression of Tnc rescues postsynaptic βPS accumulation at tnc mutant NMJs but animals have small, tnc-like boutons.
source: Paneuronal expression of Tnc rescued the postsynaptic βPS accumulation at tnc mutant NMJs; however, these animals had small, tnc-like boutons.
evidence: This is shown by rescue experiments in Figure 7A-G.

claim: Neuron-derived Tnc can engage postsynaptic βPS to form non-productive complexes that cannot restore bouton architecture.
source: Thus, neuron-derived Tnc can engage postsynaptic βPS to form non-productive complexes that cannot restore the bouton architecture.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue of βPS levels but not bouton size with neuronal Tnc expression.

claim: Low levels of muscle Tnc rescue βPS accumulation to levels exceeding control and fully restore bouton size.
source: When low levels of Tnc were provided in the muscle using a weak promoter and low rearing temperatures (Figure 7D), βPS accumulation was rescued to levels exceeding the control and bouton size was fully restored.
evidence: This is shown by rescue experiments in Figure 7D,F-G.

claim: High levels of muscle Tnc induce massive lethality and exacerbate the loss of βPS at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: In contrast, high levels of Tnc induced massive lethality and exacerbated the loss of βPS at tnc mutant NMJs; these larvae had poorly defined boutons, with almost tubular NMJ branches (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is shown by rescue experiments with high Tnc expression in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Only low levels of muscle Tnc can rescue the distribution and function of postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes, while excess muscle Tnc is toxic.
source: Together these results indicate that only low levels of muscle Tnc could rescue the distribution and function of postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes, while excess muscle Tnc is toxic.
evidence: This is concluded from the dose-dependent effects of muscle Tnc on βPS and bouton size.

claim: Neuron-derived Tnc can recruit and/or stabilize integrin but cannot form fully functional complexes.
source: On the other hand, neuron-derived Tnc can recruit and/or stabilize integrin but cannot form fully functional complexes.
evidence: This is concluded from the rescue of βPS but not bouton size with neuronal Tnc.

claim: Only low levels of muscle Tnc can fully restore the accumulation of α-Spectrin at tnc mutant NMJs.
source: In support of this interpretation, we found that only low levels of muscle Tnc could fully restore the accumulation of α-Spectrin at tnc mutant NMJs (Figure 7H–M); neuronal Tnc induced only a modest increase in synaptic α-Spectrin levels.
evidence: This is shown by rescue experiments in Figure 7H-M.

claim: Trans Tnc/integrin complexes cannot rescue bouton size, suggesting cis and trans complexes have different activities.
source: The fact that the trans Tnc/integrin complexes cannot rescue the bouton size suggests that the cis and trans complexes have different activities.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential rescue by neuronal vs. muscle Tnc.

claim: Excess neuronal Tnc reduces βPS synaptic levels to 54% from control.
source: Neuronal excess of Tnc produced a reduction of βPS synaptic levels (to 54% from control, p=0.0002, n = 23), and activities, as reflected by the reduction of bouton size compared with the control (transgene only) (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is shown by overexpression experiments in Figure 8A-F.

claim: Excess muscle Tnc practically abolishes perisynaptic βPS signals.
source: Excess Tnc in the muscles practically abolished the perisynaptic βPS signals.
evidence: This is shown by overexpression experiments in Figure 8D-E.

claim: Strong muscle overexpression of Tnc produces ribbon-like NMJs with no interbouton/bouton delimitations.
source: With strong muscle drivers (24B-Gal4 in Figure 8D, or G14-Gal4 in Figure 8—figure supplement 1), these larvae showed ribbon-like NMJs with no interbouton/bouton delimitations exceeding the severity of defects observed at tnc mutant NMJs (not shown).
evidence: This is described in the text with reference to Figure 8D.

claim: 46% of larvae with strong muscle Tnc overexpression develop into adult flies.
source: A significant number of these animals died during larval and pupal stages and only 46% (n = 211) of third instar larvae developed into adult flies.
evidence: This is stated based on counting progeny from overexpression experiments.

claim: A pulse of tnc expression in larval muscles increases Tnc levels at synaptic terminals and diminishes postsynaptic βPS signals.
source: A pulse of tnc expression in larval muscles (in larvae reared at 18°C and shifted at 25°C for 8 hr) increases the levels of Tnc at synaptic terminals and diminishes the postsynaptic βPS signals.
evidence: This is shown by pulse expression experiments in Figure 8G-H'.

claim: After a pulse of muscle Tnc expression, remaining βPS immunoreactivities appear as thin lines localized inside the boutons.
source: The remaining βPS immunoreactivities appear as thin lines (between arrows) localized inside the boutons.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8H' revealing presynaptic βPS.

claim: Excess muscle Tnc gradually disrupts postsynaptic βPS accumulation, revealing a small but clear pool of presynaptic βPS.
source: Thus, it appears that excess Tnc in the muscle gradually disrupted the postsynaptic βPS accumulation, revealing a small but clear pool of presynaptic βPS
evidence: This is concluded from the pulse expression experiment showing βPS inside boutons.

claim: Further Tnc overexpression in muscle completely disrupts both Tnc and βPS synaptic accumulation and alters bouton morphology.
source: further Tnc overexpression in the muscle completely disrupted both the Tnc and βPS synaptic accumulation and altered the boutons morphology.
evidence: This is shown by high-level overexpression experiments in Figure 8D.

claim: Excess muscle Tnc drastically reduces synaptic α-Spectrin and Adducin levels.
source: These larvae also exhibited drastically reduced levels of synaptic α-Spectrin and Adducin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown by immunostaining in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-E.

claim: Optimal levels of secreted Tnc are required for proper βPS accumulation at the NMJ.
source: Together these results indicate that optimal levels of secreted Tnc are required for proper βPS accumulation at the NMJ, which ensures normal NMJ morphology and function.
evidence: This is concluded from the dose-dependent effects of Tnc on βPS and NMJ structure.

claim: βPS integrin has a novel function in anchoring α-Spectrin at synaptic locations.
source: These experiments also uncovered a novel function for βPS integrin in anchoring α-Spectrin at synaptic locations and coupling the ECM of the synaptic cleft (Tnc) with the spectrin-based membrane skeleton.
evidence: This is concluded from the parallel loss of βPS and α-Spectrin with Tnc manipulations.

claim: Tnc-HA-coupled beads induce local accumulation of βPS at the periphery of S2R+ cells.
source: Unlike control beads (coated with an unrelated HA-tagged protein), Tnc-HA-coupled beads induced a local accumulation of βPS at the periphery of S2R + cells, in the close proximity of the beads (Figure 9A–B).
evidence: This is shown by bead recruitment assays in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Local recruitment of βPS by Tnc beads is not caused by mechanical stress.
source: This local recruitment of βPS was not caused by mechanical stress, since control beads, either alone or in clusters, did not trigger βPS accumulation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of βPS recruitment by control beads in Figure 9A.

claim: βPS recruitment by Tnc beads is dose-dependent.
source: The βPS recruitment was dose-dependent, as beads with variable Tnc-HA levels elicited proportional βPS accumulation (not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on experiments not shown in the figures.

claim: Tnc-coupled beads trigger local recruitment of αPS2 but not αPS1 integrin subunit at the surface of S2R+ cells.
source: The Tnc-coupled beads triggered local recruitment of αPS2 but not αPS1 integrin subunit at the surface of S2R+ cells (Figure 9C–D, and not shown).
evidence: This is shown by bead recruitment assays in Figure 9C-D.

claim: Tnc-HA-coupled beads induce accumulation of α-Spectrin and Adducin at bead-cell membrane interfaces.
source: Moreover, the Tnc-HA-coupled beads induced similar accumulation of α-Spectrin and Adducin at the bead-cell membrane interfaces (Figure 9E–J).
evidence: This is shown by bead recruitment assays in Figure 9E-J.

claim: Tnc triggers the local recruitment of α-Spectrin and Adducin at the cell membrane.
source: Thus Tnc triggers the local recruitment of α-Spectrin and Adducin at the cell membrane.
evidence: This is concluded from the bead recruitment experiments.

claim: Tnc provides a powerful means to recruit and/or stabilize integrin and cortical skeleton components at synaptic terminals.
source: Nonetheless, our data establish that Tnc provides a powerful means to recruit and/or stabilize integrin and cortical skeleton components at synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is concluded from all the recruitment experiments in cells and at NMJs.

claim: βPS levels are significantly elevated in S2R+ cells expressing Tnc.
source: We found that βPS levels were significantly elevated in cells expressing Tnc; also, βPS co-localized with Tnc in large intracellular aggregates, suggesting that (a) Tnc promotes βPS secretion, and that (b) βPS and Tnc likely associate during intracellular trafficking.
evidence: This is shown by transfection experiments in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: βPS co-localizes with Tnc in large intracellular aggregates in S2R+ cells.
source: We found that βPS levels were significantly elevated in cells expressing Tnc; also, βPS co-localized with Tnc in large intracellular aggregates, suggesting that (a) Tnc promotes βPS secretion, and that (b) βPS and Tnc likely associate during intracellular trafficking.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tnc promotes βPS secretion.
source: We found that βPS levels were significantly elevated in cells expressing Tnc; also, βPS co-localized with Tnc in large intracellular aggregates, suggesting that (a) Tnc promotes βPS secretion, and that (b) βPS and Tnc likely associate during intracellular trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the elevated βPS levels in Tnc-expressing cells.

claim: βPS and Tnc likely associate during intracellular trafficking.
source: We found that βPS levels were significantly elevated in cells expressing Tnc; also, βPS co-localized with Tnc in large intracellular aggregates, suggesting that (a) Tnc promotes βPS secretion, and that (b) βPS and Tnc likely associate during intracellular trafficking.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of Tnc and βPS in intracellular aggregates.

claim: Tnc depletion alters NMJ development and function and correlates with selective disruption of αPS2/βPS integrin and spectrin accumulation at synaptic terminals.
source: First, Tnc depletion altered NMJ development and function and correlated with selective disruption of αPS2/βPS integrin and spectrin accumulation at synaptic terminals.
evidence: This summarizes the findings from tnc mutant analysis throughout the manuscript.

claim: Presynaptic Tnc/integrin modulate neurotransmitter release.
source: Second, manipulation of Tnc and integrin in neurons demonstrated that presynaptic Tnc/integrin modulate neurotransmitter release (Figure 3); spectrin mutations showed similar disruptions of the presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Featherstone et al., 2001).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuronal knockdown and rescue experiments in Figure 3.

claim: Postsynaptic Tnc influences the development of postsynaptic structures (bouton size and SSR complexity).
source: Third, postsynaptic Tnc influenced the development of postsynaptic structures (bouton size and SSR complexity), similar to integrin and spectrin (Figures 3 and 4 and [Beumer et al., 1999; Pielage et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by muscle knockdown experiments in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Presynaptic Tnc/integrin limit the accumulation and function of postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes.
source: Fourth, presynaptic Tnc/integrin limited the accumulation and function of postsynaptic Tnc/integrin complexes (Figures 4, 5, 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuronal knockdown increasing postsynaptic βPS and rescue experiments.

claim: Secreted Tnc binds integrin complexes at cell membranes, but only cis complexes are biologically active.
source: Fifth, secreted Tnc bound integrin complexes at cell membranes, but only the cis complexes were biologically active (Figures 7 and 9); trans Tnc/integrin complexes can form but cannot function at synaptic terminals and instead exhibited dominant-negative activities (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue and overexpression experiments in Figures 7-9.

claim: Trans Tnc/integrin complexes can form but cannot function at synaptic terminals and exhibit dominant-negative activities.
source: Fifth, secreted Tnc bound integrin complexes at cell membranes, but only the cis complexes were biologically active (Figures 7 and 9); trans Tnc/integrin complexes can form but cannot function at synaptic terminals and instead exhibited dominant-negative activities (Figures 7 and 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by neuronal Tnc rescuing βPS but not bouton size in Figures 7-8.

claim: Tnc is a tightly regulated component of the synaptic ECM that functions in cis to recruit αPS2/βPS integrin and the spectrin-based membrane skeleton at synaptic terminals.
source: These observations support our model that Tnc is a tightly regulated component of the synaptic ECM that functions in cis to recruit αPS2/βPS integrin and the spectrin-based membrane skeleton at synaptic terminals and together modulate the NMJ development and function.
evidence: This is the overall conclusion from all the experimental data presented.
